notes.meaning: A severe food shortage struck Israel during the time of the judges, driving a man from Bethlehem to take his wife and two sons to live in neighboring Moab. Moving to a foreign land provided physical food during a drought, but it took the family away from God's covenant people. Believers can be tempted to run from hardship rather than trusting God through difficult seasons.

The man was named Elimelech, his wife was Naomi, and their sons were Mahlon and Chilion, all belonging to the clan of Ephrathah in Bethlehem. Their names carry meaning, as Elimelech means 'God is King' and Naomi means 'pleasant.' Even though they came from an honorable family line, they settled down in the pagan territory of Moab.

Elimelech died soon after their arrival, leaving Naomi as a widow with her two sons to look after in a strange country. This sudden loss left the family without its primary protector and leader. Even in painful loss, God remains near to those who suffer.

Naomi's two sons chose Moabite wives named Orpah and Ruth, and the family continued to live in Moab for about ten years. Taking foreign wives brought the young men into contact with a pagan culture and its gods. God can still work His hidden plans for good through messy family choices.

Both Mahlon and Chilion died as young men without leaving any children behind. Naomi was left completely alone without a husband or sons to care for her. In ancient times, a childless widow was left without any human protection or financial security.

Naomi heard good news that the Lord had visited His people in Judah by ending the famine and giving them food again. She and her two daughters-in-law immediately prepared to pack up and leave Moab. When God provides a way to return to His blessings, wise people take action.

Naomi set out on the road toward Judah, and both of her daughters-in-law walked with her. They initially intended to go all the way to Israel with her rather than merely walking her out of town. True family love often shows itself during times of shared grief.

Along the road, Naomi told both young women to turn around and go back to their mothers' households. She prayed that the Lord would show them the same loyal love they had shown to their late husbands and to her. She put their welfare ahead of her own comfort.

Naomi prayed that God would grant each woman peace and security in the home of a new husband. She kissed them goodbye as a parting blessing, and all three women wept aloud. Letting go of people we care about can be intensely painful.

Both Orpah and Ruth refused to leave her and insisted they would go with her to live among her people. They felt genuine affection for Naomi and wanted to share her future. Strong relationships can make people willing to leave behind what is familiar.

Naomi urged them to go home, asking why they would follow someone who had no more sons to offer them as husbands. She was referring to the ancient duty where a brother married a deceased brother's widow to raise up children. She wanted them to realize she could offer them no marital future.

Naomi explained that she was far too old to marry again and start a new family. Even if she had a husband that very night and became pregnant with baby boys, their situation would not change. She wanted them to face the hard reality of their circumstances.

Naomi asked if they could realistically wait until baby boys grew into grown men without getting married. She explained that her sorrow was far heavier for their sakes because the Lord's hand had gone out against her in judgment. She honestly acknowledged that her hardships came under the sovereign hand of God.

The women wept openly again at the thought of separating. Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye and returned to her homeland, but Ruth held on tightly and refused to let go. Hard trials reveal who is truly committed for the long haul.

Naomi pointed out that Orpah had returned to her own people and her local Moabite gods. She pressed Ruth one last time to follow her sister-in-law back home. Naomi tested Ruth's heart to make sure she was not acting on a passing impulse.

Ruth pleaded with Naomi not to send her away, promising to go wherever Naomi went and to lodge wherever she lodged. She boldly declared that Naomi's people would be her people and Naomi's God would be her God. Ruth turned her back on her native idols to trust the Lord completely.

differ.view: Ruth's conversion came solely through God's sovereign grace working in her heart to make her willing to choose Him.

notes.meaning: Ruth pledged that she would die in Naomi's land and be buried beside her in the same ground. She sealed her vow by asking the Lord to punish her severely if anything other than death separated them. True faith involves an unconditional, lifelong surrender to God and His people.

When Naomi saw that Ruth's mind was completely made up, she stopped trying to urge her to go back. Ruth's unwavering resolve brought an end to all objections. A firm decision to follow the Lord silences worldly arguments.

The two women walked together until they arrived in Bethlehem after a long journey of about fifty miles. Their arrival stirred up excitement throughout the whole town, and the local women wondered if this worn traveler could truly be Naomi. Years of hardship and grief can greatly change a person's appearance.

Naomi told the greeters not to call her 'Pleasant' anymore, but to call her Mara, which means 'bitter.' She explained that the Almighty God had dealt very bitterly with her life. It is common to feel overwhelmed by sorrow when life turns hard.

She recalled how she had left Bethlehem full of family and possessions, but the Lord had brought her back empty and destitute. She felt that the Lord had testified against her like a judge in court. Even when believers cannot see it, God is still preparing a way to restore them.

Naomi returned from the country of Moab with her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth beside her. They reached Bethlehem just as the spring barley harvest was beginning in late March or April. God brought them home at the perfect moment to receive His daily bread.
